note: complete essay: it argues, it answers an objection

sections.text: Every team I have worked on estimates in points, and every one of them has had the conversation about what a point is worth in days. The conversation always ends the same way: points are not days, and then someone divides the sprint total by ten anyway.
An estimate that is used to hold someone accountable stops being an estimate. It becomes a promise, and people price promises defensively.
sections.thin: It seems to me that there is a genuinely significant underlying problem in the way these things end up being used in practice within organisations, one that would deserve rather more serious attention than it usually gets.

sections.text: The moment a number appears on a slide next to a name, the cost of being wrong is asymmetric: too high and nobody notices, too low and you are explaining yourself in public. Every individual rationally inflates, and the aggregate is useless in a direction nobody can correct for.
sections.thin: There are good reasons to think this is what happens.

sections.text: You can watch it happen inside one team. Ours doubled its average story size over two quarters without the stories getting bigger — the only thing that changed was that the burndown started appearing in a monthly review.

The obvious answer is that this is a management failure rather than an estimation failure: estimate honestly, and push back when the number is misused. Plenty of teams do exactly that and their numbers stay usable.
sections.thin: Naturally, not everyone will share this point of view, and there are a number of arguments that point in a different direction which it would probably be dishonest to pass over entirely in the course of this discussion.

sections.text: That works while the person doing the pushing back is still there. It is a defence held by one individual against a standing incentive, and it fails on the day they leave — which is the definition of a thing that is not actually fixed.
sections.thin: But I do not think that objection really holds up.

sections.text: This only bites where estimates are visible above the team. A number that never leaves the room it was made in stays a number, and those teams should keep estimating exactly as they do.
